summary: Describes best current practices for deploying the Multicast Source Discovery Protocol with PIM-SM inside and between domains. It is a Best Current Practice document.

eli5.summary: MSDP lets different multicast areas tell each other about active senders. This gives advice on setting it up sensibly.

subtitle: How to wire up MSDP peerings between and inside PIM domains so Source Active messages pass the peer-RPF check.

tldr.problem: PIM-SM assumes a single domain, so routers in different domains cannot learn about each other's active multicast sources. MSDP fills that gap, but peerings must line up with BGP data or SA messages are dropped.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through inter-domain and intra-domain peering layouts (border routers, mesh groups, route reflectors, Anycast RPs) and shows which peer-RPF rule each one relies on.
tldr.outcome: Operators get working patterns for ASM across domains, plus advice to filter SA messages and limit SA-cache state. It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 121).

today: RFC 4611 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 121) published in August 2006. It has not been obsoleted or updated, according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Where MSDP Is Used
sections.content:
MSDP (RFC 3618) is used mainly in two ways. Between PIM domains, it conveys information about active sources in other domains. Those peerings are generally one-to-one, use the deterministic peer-RPF rules, and do not use mesh groups. One peer can have from one to hundreds of peerings, similar in scale to BGP peerings.

Within a PIM domain, MSDP is often used between Anycast RPs (RFC 3446) to synchronize information about active sources. That usually uses MSDP mesh groups of two to tens of peers, though more than ten is not typical.

Current best practice combines PIM-SM (RFC 4601) with BGP and its multiprotocol extensions (MBGP, RFC 4271 and RFC 2858) to give intra-domain and inter-domain Any Source Multicast. Because MSDP splits Internet multicast into multiple PIM domains, it also allows policy on the visibility of groups and sources.

Transit providers typically use MSDP to join the global multicast infrastructure. Edge networks can use their provider's RP, or run their own RP and connect it with MSDP so internal groups keep working if the provider has problems. Where no internal groups are needed, MSDP is often unnecessary.
sections.eli5: Routers in one area know who is sending, but routers in another area do not. MSDP lets the areas pass that news along.

sections.title: A BCP About an Experimental Protocol
sections.content:
MSDP is a widely deployed Experimental protocol with no plan to advance to Proposed Standard. The RFC gives reasons: it was meant to be temporary until the IDMR or BGMP working groups produced an inter-domain protocol, which never happened; readvertising everything every 60 seconds limits scalability; it reached nearly ubiquitous deployment as the de facto inter-domain multicast protocol in the IPv4 Internet; and no consensus could be reached on reworking it. SSM, bi-directional PIM and embedded RP for IPv6 reduced the need for a replacement.

Since BCPs must not normally reference Experimental protocols, the MBONED Working Group asked for approval under the Variance Procedure of RFC 2026, and the IESG approved it after an additional 4-week IETF Last Call.
sections.eli5: MSDP was meant to be a stopgap, but nothing better arrived, so everyone kept using it and this advice was written for it.

sections.title: Inter-domain Peering and the Peer-RPF Check
sections.content:
When two domains peer at their border routers, each domain has its own RP, typically its own AS number and one or more MBGP speakers. MSDP and MBGP are usually configured with the same directly connected next-hop peer address. For the peering to work, the first AS in the MBGP best path to the originating RP should be the same as the AS of the MSDP peer. This peer-RPF check relies on BGP AS path information, which prevents endless SA looping.

In the RFC's example, AS4 gets an SA originated by AS1 from AS2. The first AS on AS4's best path to the originating RP is AS2, which is also the sending peer's AS, so the check passes. Code that follows the latest MSDP rules relaxes this a little: it picks the peer in the closest AS along the best path to the RP, and if several peers are in the same AS, the one with the highest IP address is chosen as the RPF peer.

Peering does not have to be at the border. Providers often dedicate a few core routers to customer MSDP peerings; these usually also sit in the intra-domain mesh group and are configured for Anycast RP. The MSDP peer address should be in the same AS as the border router's MBGP peer and should be advertised via MBGP. At a multicast exchange, providers peer on a common subnet or point-to-point VLANs, each MSDP and MBGP peering with the others' directly connected exchange addresses.
sections.eli5: Each news message remembers which neighborhoods it came through. A router only believes it if it arrived from the neighbor it expected, which stops messages from circling forever.

sections.title: Peering Without BGP
sections.content:
An enterprise may keep its own RP and peer MSDP with its provider without BGP peering. MSDP normally uses BGP path information for the peer-RPF check, but the check is suspended in some cases:

  • there is only a single MSDP peer connection,
  • a default peer (default MSDP route) is configured,
  • the originating RP is directly connected,
  • a mesh group is used,
  • an implementation allows the check to use an IGP.

An enterprise typically configures a unicast default route to the provider and MSDP peers with the provider's MSDP router. If it also has internal MSDP peerings, a default MSDP peer pointing to the provider is configured on the border router. A stub site with a single provider peering uses a default peer and skips the check.
sections.eli5: Without the usual map, a small network can just say that one big neighbor is always right. That is fine when it has only that one neighbor.

sections.title: Intra-domain Peering Patterns
sections.content:
Inside a domain, the peer-RPF check uses the iBGP next hop address (an IGP can also be used), not the AS path. So the MSDP peer address must match the internal MBGP peer address. In the RFC's example, RP2 peers with Ra at 2.2.2.2 and with Rb at 3.3.3.3. An SA for 1.1.1.1 arriving from Ra passes because 2.2.2.2 is the MBGP next hop for 1.1.1.1. The same SA arriving from Rb fails, which prevents a loop.

Where few routers run MBGP, the rules are relaxed for mesh group peers, a sole MSDP peer, a default peer, peering with the originating RP, or an IGP-based check. The common choice with several peers is an MSDP mesh group: SAs from a mesh group peer are accepted without an RPF check and are not flooded to other peers in the same group, which cuts SA traffic. Mesh groups must be fully meshed.

Hierarchical mesh groups reduce the number of peerings per router with a core mesh group whose members aggregate leaf mesh groups. Do not connect mesh groups in a loop, and redundant links between a leaf group and the core also create a loop.

With route reflectors, clients must MSDP peer with the route reflector, because it is the announcer of the next hop toward the originating RP. Newer MSDP rules also allow peering with the next hop itself. With Anycast RP, several RPs share one loopback address and form a fully meshed MSDP group using a separate loopback. Unicast routing sends registers and joins to the nearest one, and if it fails, to the next nearest.
sections.eli5: Inside one network the routers check that news came from the exact neighbor their map points to. Groups of routers that all trust each other can skip that check, but must never be wired in a loop.

sections.title: Filtering and State Limits
sections.content:
MSDP state should be controlled locally at the edge where it originates, as with unicast routing state. SA origination should be filtered so only intended local sources create SAs, and speakers should filter which SAs they receive and forward. Without filters, domain-local (S,G) state, such as sources using RFC 1918 addresses or local applications on global multicast addresses, may leak to the global MSDP infrastructure. An external SA filter list is recommended.

An SA-cache state limit SHOULD be configured as a final safeguard against state spikes. Once a peering is stable, a rate limiter on creating new SA state entries may also be desirable.
sections.eli5: Only announce senders that really should be public, and cap how many announcements a router will remember, so a flood cannot overwhelm it.

viz.caption: WHERE THE PEER-RPF CHECK IS SKIPPED

cells: Only one MSDP peer connection exists
A default MSDP route is configured
The originating RP is directly connected
SAs from mesh group peers are always accepted
The implementation checks peer-RPF using an IGP
